Aside from the second and third lines, this content does not match the provided `foo` function.

The first line was intended to add 10 to `x`; your solution adds only 1 to `x`. The fourth line was the final instruction of the `foo` function and was intended to assign `x` to `a[i]`. Instead, your solution increments `i` a second time and then sets `x` to `y + 1` for some reason, and never interacts with the array `a` whatsoever.

This will result in your solution's output not matching the intended solution.

As an additional note, `i = i + 1` is not conventional incrementation. There is no reason not to use `i++` (as post-increment was used in the given `foo` function) or at least `++i`, which, in this context, has the same effect but works faster.

See comment on `foo_val`—this implementation performs the same random instructions as `foo_val` rather than the instructions in the provided `foo` function. Your `foo_ref` output is completely different from the intended output as a result.

There is no reason to create additional pointers to the addresses of the actuals `real_x` and `real_y` here. The following has the same effect but avoids wasting time and space on these pointers:

```c++
int x = real_x;     // x is now a copy of real_x
int y = real_y;     // y is now a copy of real_y
```

Since this copy initializes `x` and `y` to the values of `real_x` and `real_y` respectively, it has the same effect.
See comments on `foo_val` and `foo_ref`—these instructions differ completely from the provided `foo` function and thus provide completely different output.

If the body of the provided `foo` function matched your `foo_val` implementation, this would be a correct representation of pass-by-name. Good job using the thunks properly.

However—like with `foo_val`, `foo_ref`, and `foo_val_result`—these instructions are entirely different from the `foo` function that the instructions provided and asked you to represent, so this too will provide fully incorrect output.
